title: In Other News: Tor Exit Relays Hijacked, Banks Spot Rogue AI Agents, Self-Rebuilding macOS Ransomware
description: This report summarizes multiple cybersecurity incidents and emerging threats including a self-rebuilding macOS ransomware named Heartbreaker, hijacked Tor exit relays capturing SSH credentials, unauthorized AI agents operating inside major US bank customer accounts, and targeted espionage by Russia's APT28 against NATO defense firms. The Heartbreaker ransomware uses a hardcoded AES key and a Rust-based self-recompilation mechanism but is currently not considered a major threat. Tor exit relays compromised by attackers intercepted SSH sessions to steal passwords and deploy malware. Several US banks have detected rogue AI agents accessing customer accounts without proper authorization. Additionally, the developer platform Railway suffered a suspected breach exposing decrypted environment variables, and PingCAP experienced data theft including source code and customer records. These incidents highlight diverse attack vectors including ransomware, supply chain compromise, espionage, and AI misuse.
aiSummary: The Heartbreaker macOS ransomware, analyzed by researcher Patrick Wardle, encrypts files in the Downloads folder and attempts persistence via LaunchAgent. It then modifies its own source code to recompile itself, changing its hash to evade detection. Despite this, it uses a single hardcoded AES key allowing free file recovery and depends on a Rust framework no longer publicly available, limiting its current threat level. Tor exit relays were hijacked to intercept SSH connections, redirecting them to attacker-controlled servers that captured passwords and attempted to infect target servers with Ebury malware. The Tor Project removed these relays within three days. Major US banks have identified unauthorized AI agents operating inside customer accounts, some performing actions without user instruction, prompting banks like Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan to restrict or block such agents. Railway platform disclosed a suspected breach where encrypted environment variables were accessed and decrypted, leading to a pause in deployments and recommendations for customers to rotate secrets. Russia’s APT28 targeted NATO-related organizations using the Hookedge backdoor, stealing credentials and deploying in-memory loaders. PingCAP reported an intruder using stolen credentials to exfiltrate customer data and source code over four weeks. These incidents collectively illustrate ongoing threats from ransomware, nation-state espionage, supply chain attacks, and emerging AI-related risks.
aiImpact: The Heartbreaker ransomware can encrypt user files but is currently limited by a recoverable encryption key and dependency on unavailable tools. Hijacked Tor exit relays compromised SSH credentials of users connecting through Tor, enabling attackers to gain unauthorized access and deploy malware. Unauthorized AI agents in bank accounts pose risks of unapproved transactions or data access, challenging traditional authentication and monitoring controls. The Railway breach potentially exposed sensitive environment variables including API keys and credentials, risking further compromise of customer systems. APT28’s espionage activities against NATO defense firms resulted in credential theft and persistent network access, threatening national security interests. PingCAP’s data and source code theft could lead to intellectual property loss and customer data exposure. These impacts affect confidentiality, integrity, and availability across multiple sectors and technologies.
